nodes.name: $\sigma\pi\alpha$ is strongly normalizing
nodes.statement: $\sigma\pi\alpha$ is strongly normalizing (on the sets of terms, substitutions, and judgements of the form $\Gamma\vdash M$).
conclusions: $\sigma\pi\alpha$ is strongly normalizing (on the sets of terms, substitutions, and judgements of the form $\Gamma\vdash M$)

nodes.name: Proof that $\sigma\pi\alpha$ is strongly normalizing (postponed)
nodes.statement: The proof is postponed until Section~\ref{section9}.
nodes.statement_short: Deferred to the semantic-labelling argument of the final section.

nodes.name: One-step $\beta$-reduction on the set of pure name-free terms
nodes.statement: (One-step $\beta$-reduction on the set of pure name-free terms).\\[5pt] \ruleone{U\arrow_{Beta}V}{U\arrow_{\beta}\sigma(V) \using{\quad(U \text{ is pure})}}\\[5pt] (the compatible closure, of course).

nodes.name: $Beta$-steps descend to $\beta$-steps on $\sigma$-normal forms
nodes.statement: If $U\arrow_{Beta}V$, then $\sigma(U)\arrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$, where $\arrow^*_{\beta}$ is the reflexive closure of $\,\arrow_{\beta}$.
conclusions: $\sigma(U)\arrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$, where $\arrow^*_{\beta}$ is the reflexive closure of $\,\arrow_{\beta}$

nodes.name: Proof that $Beta$-steps descend to $\beta$-steps
nodes.statement: See~\cite{Abadi}, Lemma 3.5.
nodes.statement_short: Deferred to the cited source.

nodes.name: $\lambda\pi$-reductions project onto $\lambda\sigma$-reductions
nodes.statement: Suppose \\ $\begin{array}{l} \Gamma\vdash M\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma\vdash L;\\ (\Gamma\vdash M)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} U;\\ (\Sigma\vdash L)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} V; \end{array}$\\[5pt] then $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh}\sigma(V)$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $\lambda\pi$ reduction of judgements is mirrored by a $\lambda\sigma$ reduction of the corresponding $\sigma$-normal forms.

nodes.name: Proof that $\lambda\pi$-reductions project onto $\lambda\sigma$-reductions
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction over the length of the reduction sequence $\Gamma\vdash M\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma\vdash L$. If this length is equal to $0$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, suppose this sequence has the form \\ $\Gamma\vdash M\ri\ldots\ri\Delta\vdash N\ri\Sigma\vdash L$,\\ where $(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} W$ and $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh}\sigma(W)$.\\ If the reduction step $\Delta\vdash N\ri\Sigma\vdash L$ belongs to $\sigma\pi\alpha$, everything is all right, because $\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case. Indeed, $\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable by Lemma~\ref{poleznaya}. $\Delta\vdash N$ and $\Sigma\vdash L$ are derivable by Subject reduction. Take any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Sigma\vdash L$ (this normal form exists by Theorem ~\ref{SN} and are derivable too) and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to get $ W\overset{\sigma}{\twoh}\sigma(V)$.\\ If $\Delta\vdash N\ri_{Beta}\Sigma\vdash L$, then $W\arrow_{Beta}V$, because any $Beta$-redex in $N$ corresponds to some $Beta$-redex in $W$, hence $\sigma(W)\arrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the reduction length, separating $\sigma\pi\alpha$-steps (which do not change the $\sigma$-normal form) from $Beta$-steps.

nodes.name: Lifting $\lambda\sigma$-reductions back to $\lambda\pi$
nodes.statement: Suppose \\ $\begin{array}{l} (\Gamma\vdash M) \boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} U;\\ U\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh}V; \end{array}$\\ then there is $\Sigma\vdash L$ such that\\ $\begin{array}{l} \Gamma\vdash M\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma\vdash L;\\ \Sigma\vdash L \text{ is a } \sigma\pi\alpha\text{-normal form (with respect to $\overset{\sigma\pi\alpha}{\ri\ri}$)};\\ (\Sigma\vdash L)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V). \end{array}$
nodes.statement_short: Any $\lambda\sigma$ reduction of the translation is realised by a $\lambda\pi$ reduction of the original judgement.
conclusions: then there is $\Sigma\vdash L$ such that\\ $\begin{array}{l} \Gamma\vdash M\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma\vdash L;\\ \Sigma\vdash L \text{ is a } \sigma\pi\alpha\text{-normal form (with respect to $\overset{\sigma\pi\alpha}{\ri\ri}$)};\\ (\Sigma\vdash L)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V). \end{array}$

nodes.name: Proof of the lifting of $\lambda\sigma$-reductions
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction over the length of the reduction sequence $U\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh}V$. \\[5pt] Case 1: If this length is equal to $0$, take any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Gamma\vdash M$ as $\Sigma\vdash L$ and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem}. \\[5pt] Case 2: Suppose this sequence has the form $U\arrow \ldots\arrow W\arrow V$ and the sequence $U\arrow \ldots\arrow W$ satisfies the statement of the theorem, i.e.:\\ $\Gamma\vdash M \overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Delta\vdash N$ for some $\Delta\vdash N$, where $\Delta\vdash N$ is a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form and $(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(W)$.\\[3pt] If the reduction step $W\arrow V$ belongs to $\sigma$, everything is all right, because $\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case and we can use $\Delta\vdash N$ as $\Sigma\vdash L$. \\[3pt] If $W\arrow_{Beta}V$, then $\sigma(W)\arrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}. If $\sigma(W)$ coincides with $\sigma(V)$, everything is all right. Otherwise, suppose $\sigma(W)\arrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ has the form $\sigma(W)\arrow_{Beta}W'\overset{\sigma}{\twoh}\sigma(V)$. Any $Beta$-redex in $\sigma(W)$ corresponds to some $Beta$-redex in $N$. Contracting this redex in $N$, we obtain\\ $\Delta\vdash N\ri_{Beta}\Delta\vdash N'$ and $(\Delta\vdash N')\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}W'$, for some $N'$. Take any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta\vdash N'$ as $\Sigma\vdash L$, then use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to obtain\\ $(\Sigma\vdash L)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V)$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the length of the $\lambda\sigma$ reduction, with the base case supplied by the projection theorem.

nodes.name: Extended name-free terms and substitutions
nodes.statement: Only in this section, we use the following notation: the symbols $U,V,W$ range over \emph{extended name-free terms} and the symbols $u,v,w$ range over \emph{extended name-free substitutions}. The sets of extended name-free terms and extended name-free substitutions are defined inductively as follows: \begin{align*} U,V::&= \underline{n} \mid UV \mid \lambda U \mid u\ci U \\ u,v::&= id \mid \pi \mid \langle u\mi V \rangle \mid u\ci v \end{align*} ($n\in N, n\geqslant 1$)
nodes.statement_short: Like name-free terms but built from all numerals $\underline{n}$ rather than from $1$ alone.

nodes.name: $\lambda\lambda\underline{2}(\pi\ci\underline{1})$ is an extended nameless term
nodes.statement: $\lambda\lambda\underline{2}(\pi\ci\underline{1})$ is an extended nameless term.

nodes.name: Pure extended nameless term
nodes.statement: An extended nameless term $U$ is called \emph{pure} iff it does not contain sub-terms of the form $u\ci U$.
differentia: it does not contain sub-terms of the form $u\ci U$

nodes.name: Name-free judgement
nodes.statement: A \emph{name-free judgement} is an expression of the form $m\vdash U$ or of the form $m\vdash u$, where $m\in N,m\geqslant 0$.
differentia: of the form $m\vdash U$ or of the form $m\vdash u$, where $m\in N,m\geqslant 0$

nodes.name: Notation $\Rightarrow$ for name-free judgements
nodes.statement: $(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow(m\vdash U)$ is shorthand for ``the name-free judgement $m\vdash U$ corresponds to the judgement $\Gamma\vdash M$." \\ $(\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta)\Rightarrow(m\vdash u)$ is shorthand for ``the name-free judgement $m\vdash u$ corresponds to the judgement $\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta$."

nodes.name: Context length $|\Gamma|$
nodes.statement: By $|\Gamma|$ denote the length of $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: The rules of correspondence between judgements and name-free judgements
nodes.statement: (The rules of correspondence between judgements and name-free judgements).\\ $ \begin{array}{ll} (i)& (\Gamma,\x\vdash \x)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma,\x|\vdash \underline{1}) \\[5pt] (ii)& \ruleone{(\Gamma\vdash \x)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash \underline{n})}{(\Gamma,\y\vdash \x)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma,\y| \vdash \underline{n+1})\using {\quad(\x\neq \y)}}\\[20pt] (iii)& \ruletwo{(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash U)}{(\Gamma\vdash N)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash V)}{(\Gamma\vdash MN)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash UV)}\\[15pt] (iv)& \ruleone{(\Gamma,\x\vdash M)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma,\x| \vdash U)}{(\Gamma\vdash\lambda \x.M)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash \lambda U) }\\[15pt] (v)& \ruletwo{(\Gamma\vdash s \tri\Delta)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash u) }{(\Delta\vdash M)\Rightarrow (|\Delta| \vdash U)}{(\Gamma\vdash s \ci M)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash u \ci U)}\\[15pt] (vi)& (\Gamma\vdash id \tri\Gamma)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash id ) \\[5pt] (vii)& (\Gamma,\x\vdash\pi_{\x} \tri\Gamma)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma,\x| \vdash \pi ) \\[5pt] (viii)& \ruletwo{(\Gamma\vdash s \tri\Delta)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash u ) }{(\Gamma\vdash N)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash V)}{(\Gamma\vdash \langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle \tri\Delta ,\x)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash\langle u\mi V\rangle )}\\[15pt] (ix)& \ruletwo{(\Gamma\vdash s \tri\Delta)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash u) }{(\Delta\vdash q \tri\Sigma)\Rightarrow (|\Delta| \vdash v ) }{(\Gamma \vdash s \ci q \tri\Sigma)\Rightarrow (|\Gamma| \vdash u \ci v )}\\ \end{array} $
nodes.statement_short: Nine rules translating a judgement into a name-free judgement $|\Gamma|\vdash U$, recording the context length alongside the De Bruijn term.
nodes.definiendum: The rules of correspondence between judgements and name-free judgements

nodes.name: The name-free index equals the context length
nodes.statement: If $(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow(m\vdash U)$, then $m=|\Gamma|$.\\ If $(\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta)\Rightarrow(m\vdash u)$, then $m=|\Gamma|$.

nodes.name: $(x\vdash x)\Rightarrow (1 \vdash \underline{1})$
nodes.statement: $$ (x\vdash x)\Rightarrow (1 \vdash \underline{1}) $$

nodes.name: $(x,y \vdash x)\Rightarrow (2 \vdash \underline{2})$
nodes.statement: $$ \ruleone{(x\vdash x)\Rightarrow (1 \vdash \underline{1})}{(x,y \vdash x)\Rightarrow (2 \vdash \underline{2})} $$

nodes.name: $(x,y \vdash \pi_y\ci x) \Rightarrow (2 \vdash \pi\ci \underline{1})$
nodes.statement: $$ \ruletwo{(x,y \vdash \pi_y\tri x) \Rightarrow (2 \vdash \pi)}{(x \vdash x) \Rightarrow (1 \vdash \underline{1})}{(x,y \vdash \pi_y\ci x) \Rightarrow (2 \vdash \pi\ci \underline{1})} $$
nodes.statement_short: The name-free judgement records both the context length $2$ and the shifted numeral.

nodes.name: $\alpha$-equivalence
nodes.statement: ($\alpha$-equivalence).\\ We say that $\Gamma\vdash M$ is $\alpha$-\emph{equal} to $\Delta\vdash N$ and write\\ $(\Gamma\vdash M)\alp(\Delta\vdash N)$ iff\\ $(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow (m\vdash U)$ and\\ $(\Delta\vdash N)\Rightarrow (m\vdash U)$, for some $m,U$.
nodes.statement_short: Two judgements are $\alpha$-equal when they translate to the same name-free judgement.

nodes.name: $(x,y\vdash\pi_y\ci x)\alp (x,x\vdash\pi_x\ci x)$
nodes.statement: $ $\\ $(x,y\vdash\pi_y\ci x)\Rightarrow (2\vdash \pi\ci \underline{1})$\\ $(x,x\vdash\pi_x\ci x)\Rightarrow (2\vdash \pi\ci \underline{1})$\\ $(x,y\vdash\pi_y\ci x)\alp (x,x\vdash\pi_x\ci x)$
nodes.statement_short: Repeating a context variable is $\alpha$-invisible once the shift is made explicit.

nodes.name: $(x\vdash\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x)\alp (x\vdash\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x)$
nodes.statement: $ $\\ $(x\vdash\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x)\Rightarrow (1\vdash \lambda\pi\ci \underline{1})$\\ $(x\vdash\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x)\Rightarrow (1\vdash \lambda\pi\ci \underline{1})$\\ $(x\vdash\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x)\alp (x\vdash\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x)$
nodes.statement_short: A binder that shadows a free variable is $\alpha$-equal to one that does not.

nodes.name: $(\vdash\lambda x.\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x)\alp (\vdash\lambda x.\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x)$
nodes.statement: $ $\\ $(\vdash\lambda x.\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x)\Rightarrow (0\vdash \lambda\lambda\pi\ci \underline{1})$\\ $(\vdash\lambda x.\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x)\Rightarrow (0\vdash \lambda\lambda\pi\ci \underline{1})$\\ $(\vdash\lambda x.\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x)\alp (\vdash\lambda x.\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x)$
nodes.statement_short: The closed doubly-shadowing term is $\alpha$-equal to the standard one.

nodes.name: $\backsimeq$ does not imply $\alp$
nodes.statement: $ $\\ $(x,y\vdash x) \backsimeq (x,y\vdash\pi_y\ci x)$\\ $(x,y\vdash x)\,{\not\alp} (x,y\vdash\pi_y\ci x)$
nodes.statement_short: $(x,y\vdash x)$ and $(x,y\vdash\pi_y\ci x)$ are $\backsimeq$-related but not $\alpha$-equal.

nodes.name: Name-free correspondence implies derivability
nodes.statement: If $(\Gamma\vdash M)\Rightarrow(m\vdash U)$, then $\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable.

nodes.name: Proof that name-free correspondence implies derivability
nodes.statement: The proof is straightforward, see Definition~\ref{defsequentsder} and Definition~\ref{deftransfer}.
nodes.statement_short: Asserted as straightforward: the correspondence rules mirror the inference rules.

nodes.name: $\alpha$-equal judgements are derivable
nodes.statement: If $(\Gamma\vdash M)\alp(\Delta\vdash N)$, then $\Gamma\vdash M$ and $\Delta\vdash N$ are derivable.

nodes.name: Comparison of $\alp$ and $\backsimeq$
nodes.statement: $ $\\ Suppose $(\Gamma\vdash M)\alp(\Delta\vdash N)$; then $(\Gamma\vdash M)\backsimeq(\Delta\vdash N)$.\\ Suppose $(\Gamma\vdash M)\backsimeq(\Delta\vdash N)$, where $|\Gamma|=|\Delta|$ and both $M$ and $N$ are pure; then $(\Gamma\vdash M)\alp(\Delta\vdash N)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha$-equality implies $\backsimeq$, and the converse holds for pure subjects in contexts of equal length.

nodes.name: Proof of the comparison of $\alp$ and $\backsimeq$
nodes.statement: The proof of the first part is straightforward, see Definition~\ref{transfer} and Definition~\ref{deftransfer}. To prove the second part, recall that each pure term is constructed from variables by using application and abstraction. This prevents such counterexamples as Example~\ref{counterexample}.
nodes.statement_short: The first part is direct; the second uses that pure terms are built only from variables, which blocks the counterexample.

nodes.name: $\sigma\pi\alpha$ is confluent
nodes.statement: Suppose\\ $\begin{array}{l} (\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\alp(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2);\\ \Gamma_1\vdash M_1\overset{\sigma\pi\alpha}{\ri\ri}\Delta_1\vdash N_1;\\ \Gamma_2\vdash M_2\overset{\sigma\pi\alpha}{\ri\ri}\Delta_2\vdash N_2; \end{array}$\\ then there are $\Sigma_1\vdash L_1$ and $\Sigma_2\vdash L_2$ such that\\ $\begin{array}{l} \Delta_1\vdash N_1\overset{\sigma\pi\alpha}{\ri\ri}\Sigma_1\vdash L_1;\\ \Delta_2\vdash N_2\overset{\sigma\pi\alpha}{\ri\ri}\Sigma_2\vdash L_2;\\ (\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\alp(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2). \end{array}$
nodes.statement_short: Two $\sigma\pi\alpha$ reductions from $\alpha$-equal judgements can be joined up to $\alpha$-equality.

nodes.name: Proof that $\sigma\pi\alpha$ is confluent
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\backsimeq(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)$.\\ Suppose $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$ and $(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$.\\ Let $\Sigma_1\vdash L_1$ be any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta_1\vdash N_1$ and let $\Sigma_2\vdash L_2$ be any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta_2\vdash N_2$. By Theorem~\ref{maintheorem}, we have\\ $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(U)$ and $(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(U)$, hence\\ $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\backsimeq(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$. Note that $L_1$ and $L_2$ are pure (Theorem~\ref{pure}). Note that $|\Sigma_1|=|\Sigma_2|=|\Gamma_1|=|\Gamma_2|$ (because all reductions preserve lengths of contexts). By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have\\ $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\alp(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Push both reductions to $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal forms, which the projection theorem shows have the same translation $\sigma(U)$.

nodes.name: $\lambda\pi$ is confluent
nodes.statement: Suppose\\ $\begin{array}{l} (\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\alp(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2);\\ \Gamma_1\vdash M_1\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Delta_1\vdash N_1;\\ \Gamma_2\vdash M_2\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Delta_2\vdash N_2; \end{array}$\\ then there are $\Sigma_1\vdash L_1$ and $\Sigma_2\vdash L_2$ such that\\ $\begin{array}{l} \Delta_1\vdash N_1\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma_1\vdash L_1;\\ \Delta_2\vdash N_2\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma_2\vdash L_2;\\ (\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\alp(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2). \end{array}$
nodes.statement_short: Two $\lambda\pi$ reductions from $\alpha$-equal judgements can be joined up to $\alpha$-equality.

nodes.name: Proof that $\lambda\pi$ is confluent
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\backsimeq(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)$.\\ Suppose $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$; $(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$;\\ $(\Delta_1\vdash N_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}V_1$; and $(\Delta_2\vdash N_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}V_2$.\\ By Theorem~\ref{theorem33}, we have $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} \sigma(V_1)$ and $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} \sigma(V_2)$.\\ We know that $\lambda\sigma$ is confluent, hence $\sigma(V_1)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} V$ and $\sigma(V_2)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} V$ for some $V$. Therefore $V_1\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} V$ and $V_2\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} V$. By Theorem~\ref{theorem44}, we have $\Sigma_1\vdash L_1$ and $\Sigma_2\vdash L_2$ such that\\ $\begin{array}{l} \Delta_1\vdash N_1\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma_1\vdash L_1;\\ \Delta_2\vdash N_2\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma_2\vdash L_2;\\ \Sigma_1\vdash L_1 \text{ is a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form};\\ \Sigma_2\vdash L_2 \text{ is a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form};\\ (\Sigma_1\vdash V_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V);\\ (\Sigma_2\vdash V_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V). \end{array}$\\[5pt] Hence $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\backsimeq(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$. Note that $L_1$ and $L_2$ are pure (Theorem~\ref{pure}). Note that $|\Sigma_1|=|\Sigma_2|=|\Gamma_1|=|\Gamma_2|$ (because all reductions preserve lengths of contexts). By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have\\ $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\alp(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer both reductions to $\lambda\sigma$, join them there by confluence of $\lambda\sigma$, and lift the joining reductions back.

nodes.name: The set $\Lambda\pi$ of derivable judgements
nodes.statement: By $\Lambda\pi$ denote the set of derivable judgements of the form $\Gamma\vdash M$.

nodes.name: The relation $\sqsubseteq$ on sequences of sets
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{A} \sqsubseteq \mathcal{B}$ is shorthand for ``$\mathcal{A}_i\subseteq\bigcup_{j\geqslant i}\mathcal{B}_j$ for all $i\geqslant 1$".

nodes.name: $\la\{y\},\emptyset,\ldots\ra\sqsubseteq\la\emptyset,\{y\},\emptyset,\ldots\ra$
nodes.statement: $\langle\{y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle\sqsubseteq\langle\emptyset,\{y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle$

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $O_{\lambda \x}$ and $O_{\pi}$ with respect to $\sqsubseteq$
nodes.statement: $O_{\lambda \x}$ and $O_{\pi}$ are monotone operators with respect to $\sqsubseteq$ (for any $\x$).
conclusions: $O_{\lambda \x}$ and $O_{\pi}$ are monotone operators with respect to $\sqsubseteq$ (for any $\x$)

nodes.name: Proof of $\sqsubseteq$-monotonicity of $O_{\lambda \x}$ and $O_{\pi}$
nodes.statement: The proof is straightforward.
nodes.statement_short: Asserted as straightforward: both operators only shift and unite levels.

nodes.name: $\sqsubseteq$-monotonicity of union of sequences
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{A}\cup \mathcal{B}$ is monotone in both arguments with respect to $\sqsubseteq$.
conclusions: $\mathcal{A}\cup \mathcal{B}$ is monotone in both arguments with respect to $\sqsubseteq$

nodes.name: Proof of $\sqsubseteq$-monotonicity of union
nodes.statement: The proof is straightforward.
nodes.statement_short: Asserted as straightforward: union is computed level-wise.

nodes.name: $\sqsubseteq$-monotonicity of $O_s$
nodes.statement: $O_s$ is monotone with respect to $\sqsubseteq$ for any $s$.
conclusions: $O_s$ is monotone with respect to $\sqsubseteq$ for any $s$.

nodes.name: Reduction does not increase free variables in the $\sqsubseteq$ order
nodes.statement: If $M_1\arrow M_2$, then $FV(M_2)\sqsubseteq FV(M_1)$. If $s_1\arrow s_2$, then $O_{s_2}(\mathcal{A})\sqsubseteq O_{s_1}(\mathcal{A})$ for any $\mathcal{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every one-step reduction can only push free occurrences to higher levels.

nodes.name: Proof that reduction does not increase free variables
nodes.statement:
The proof is straightforward, but tedious. For example, consider\ $  egin{array}{lll} \mathbf{(Abs)} & s\ci \lambda \x.Mightarrow\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M & \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{ll} FV(\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M) & \ =FV(\lambda \x.((\pi_{\x}\ci s)\ci\lambda \x.M)\x) & (Lemma~ef{corollary3})\ =FV(\lambda \x.(\pi_{\x}\ci s\ci\lambda \x.M)\x) & (Lemma~ef{corollary23})\ =O_{\lambda \x}(O_{\pi}(FV (s\ci\lambda \x.M)) igcup FV(\x)) & \ =O_{\lambda \x}(\la\{\x\},FV_1(s\ci\lambda \x.M),FV_2(s\ci\lambda \x.M),\ldotsa) & \ =FV(s\ci\lambda \x.M) \end{array}$\ $ egin{array}{lll} \mathbf{(App)} & s\ci MN ightarrow(s\ci M)(s\ci N) & \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{l} FV(s\ci MN) \ =O_s(FV(MN))\ =O_s(FV(M)\cup FV(N))\ \supseteq O_s(FV(M))\cup O_s(FV(N))\ =FV(s\ci M)\cup FV(s\ci N)\ =FV((s\ci M)(s\ci N)) \end{array}$\ $  egin{array}{lll} \mathbf{(ConsVar)} & \langle s\mi N\is \xangle\ci \xightarrow N & \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{l} FV(\langle s\mi N\is \xangle\ci \x)\ =O_{\langle s\mi N\is \xangle}(FV(\x))\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(FV(\x)))\cup FV(N)\ \supseteq FV(N) \end{array}$\ $  egin{array}{lll} \mathbf{(New)} & \langle s\mi N\is \xangle\ci \yightarrow s\ci \y & (\x
eq \y) \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{l} FV(\langle s\mi N\is \xangle\ci \y)\ =O_{\langle s\mi N\is \xangle}(FV(\y))\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(FV(\y)))\cup FV(N)\ \supseteq O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(FV(\y)))\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(\langle\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldotsangle)\ =O_s(\langle\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldotsangle)\ =O_s(FV(\y))\ =FV(s\ci \y) \end{array}$\ $ egin{array}{lll} \mathbf{(ConsShift)} & \langle s\mi N\is \xangle\ci \pi_{\x}ightarrow s & \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{l} O_{\langle s\mi N\is \xangle\ci \pi_{\x}}(\mathcal{A})\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(O_{\pi}(\mathcal{A})))\cup FV(N)\ \supseteq O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(O_{\pi}(\mathcal{A})))\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(\langle\emptyset,\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2,\ldotsangle)\ =O_s(\langle\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2,\ldotsangle)\ =O_s(\mathcal{A}) \end{array}$\ $  egin{array}{lll} \mathbf{(Map)} & s\ci \langle q\mi N\is \xangleightarrow\langle s\ci q \mi s\ci N\is \xangle & \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{l} O_{s\,\ci \langle q\mi N\is \xangle}(\mathcal{A})\ =O_s(O_{\langle q\mi N\is \xangle}(\mathcal{A}))\ =O_s(O_q(O_{\lambda \x}(\mathcal{A}))\cup FV(N))\ \supseteq O_s(O_q(O_{\lambda \x}(\mathcal{A})))\cup O_s(FV(N))\ =O_{s\ci q}(O_{\lambda \x}(\mathcal{A}))\cup FV(s\ci N)\ =O_{\langle s\ci q \mi s\ci N\is \xangle}(\mathcal{A}) \end{array}$\ $  egin{array}{lll}  oldsymbol{(\pi_1)} & \pi_{\x}\ci \yightarrow \y & (\x
eq \y) \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{l} FV(\pi_{\x}\ci \y)\ =\langle\emptyset,\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldotsangle\ \sqsupseteq \langle\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldotsangle\ =FV(\y) \end{array}$ \ $  egin{array}{lll}  oldsymbol{(\pi_2)} & (s\ci\pi_{\x})\ci \yightarrow s\ci \y & (\x
eq \y) \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{l} FV((s\ci\pi_{\x})\ci \y)\ =O_s(O_{\pi}(FV(\y)))\ = O_s(\langle\emptyset,\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldotsangle)\ \sqsupseteq O_s(\langle\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldotsangle)\ =FV(s\ci \y) \end{array}$\ $ egin{array}{lll}  oldsymbol{(\alpha_1)} & \lambda \x.Mightarrow\lambda \y.\langle\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \xangle\ci M & (*) \end{array} $\ $ egin{array}{ll} FV(\lambda \y.\langle\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \xangle\ci M )\ =FV(\lambda \y.(\pi_{\y}\ci\lambda \x.M)\y) & (Lemma~ef{corollary3})\ =O_{\lambda \y}(O_{\pi}(FV(\lambda \x.M)) igcup FV(\y)) & \ =O_{\lambda \y}(\la\{\y\},FV_1(\lambda \x.M),FV_2(\lambda \x.M),\ldotsa) & \ =FV(\lambda \x.M) \end{array} $\[3pt] In addition, it is necessary to prove that all operations from Definition~ef{pervoe} are in some sense monotone, but this is not difficult.
nodes.statement_short: Rule-by-rule computation of $FV$ (or of $O_s$) on both sides of each rewrite rule.

nodes.name: $FV$ is invariant under the $Abs$ rule
nodes.statement: $FV(s\ci\lambda \x.M)=FV(\lambda \x.\!\Uparrow_{\x}\!(s) \ci M)$

nodes.name: $FV$ is invariant under the iterated $Abs$ rule
nodes.statement: $FV(s\ci\lambda \Delta.M)=FV(\lambda \Delta. \!\Uparrow_{\Delta}\!(s) \ci M)$

nodes.name: Reduction creates no new free variables
nodes.statement: If $M\arrow N$, then $\bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(N)\subseteq \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(M)$.

nodes.name: Signature of the rewriting system $R$
nodes.statement: The signature of $R$ contains:\\ $ \begin{array}{ll} M,N,L,\ldots & \text{variables};\\ s,q,r,\ldots & \text{variables};\\ x,y,z,\ldots & \text{constants};\\ id,\pi_x,\pi_y,\pi_z,\ldots &\text{constants};\\ \lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z,\ldots & \text{functional symbols of arity one};\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda} x,\boldsymbol{\lambda} y,\boldsymbol{\lambda} z,\ldots & \text{functional symbols of arity one};\\ \cdot\mi\circ & \text{functional symbols of arity two};\\ \la -\mi -\is x\ra,\la -\mi -\is y\ra,\la -\mi -\is z\ra,\ldots & \text{functional symbols of arity two}. \end{array} $ \\[5pt] We will omit $\cdot$, which denotes application. The sets of ground terms and ground substitutions of $R$ are defined inductively as follows: \begin{align*} M,N::&= \x \mid MN \mid \lambda \x. M \mid\boldsymbol{\lambda} \x. M\mid s\ci M \\ s,q::&= id \mid \pi_{\x} \mid \langle s\mi N\is \x \rangle \mid s\ci q \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A two-sorted signature adding a second, black abstraction symbol $\boldsymbol{\lambda} \x$ alongside $\lambda \x$.

nodes.name: The rewriting system $R$
nodes.statement:
(The rewriting system $R$).\[5pt] $  egin{array}{lll} (Abs1) & s\ci \lambda \x.Mightarrow\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M &\ (Abs2) & s\ci  oldsymbol{\lambda} \x.Mightarrow oldsymbol{\lambda} \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M &\ (Abs3) & s\ci \lambda \x.Mightarrow oldsymbol{\lambda} \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M &\ (Abs4) & s\ci  oldsymbol{\lambda} \x.Mightarrow\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M &\ (App) & s\ci MNightarrow(s\ci M)(s\ci N) &\ (ConsVar) & \langle s\mi N\is \xangle\ci \xightarrow N &\ (New) & \langle s\mi N\is \xangle\ci \yightarrow s\ci \y & (\x

nodes.statement_short: The $\sigma\pi\alpha$ rules with $Abs$ split into $Abs1$--$Abs4$ according to the colour of the abstraction, plus $\alpha$ and the bleaching rule $\xi$.

nodes.name: $FV$ for black abstractions
nodes.statement: To each term $M$ we assign $FV(M)$ as in Definition~\ref{FV} with the additional case: \\ $\begin{array}{l} FV(\boldsymbol{\lambda} \x.M)=FV(\lambda \x.M)=O_{\lambda \x}(FV(M)) \end{array}$

nodes.name: $R$-reduction does not increase free variables
nodes.statement: If $M_1\overset{R}{\arrow}M_2$, then $FV(M_2)\sqsubseteq FV(M_1)$.

nodes.name: Proof that $R$-reduction does not increase free variables
nodes.statement: See Lemma~\ref{subfreevar}.
nodes.statement_short: The colour-blind computation of $FV$ makes this the earlier $\sigma\pi\alpha$ lemma verbatim.

nodes.name: Restatement of the side condition $(*)$
nodes.statement: The restriction $(*)$ in Definition~\ref{lambdapi} can be written as\\ $ \begin{array}{ll} (*) & \x \in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(\lambda \x.M);\quad \y\notin \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(\lambda \y.\langle\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\rangle\ci M )\\ \end{array} $
nodes.statement_short: The freshness condition on $\alpha_1$ may equivalently be tested on the reduct.
conclusions: The restriction $(*)$ in Definition~\ref{lambdapi} can be written as\\ $ \begin{array}{ll} (*) & \x \in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(\lambda \x.M);\quad \y\notin \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(\lambda \y.\langle\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\rangle\ci M )\\ \end{array} $

nodes.name: Proof of the restatement of $(*)$
nodes.statement: $FV(\lambda \y.\langle\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\rangle\ci M )=FV(\lambda \x.M) $ by Lemma~\ref{subfreevar} (the case $\alpha_1$).
nodes.statement_short: The $\alpha_1$ case of the free-variable lemma shows both sides have the same $FV$.

nodes.name: The blackening $M^*$
nodes.statement: By $M^*$ denote the term $M$ in which all sub-terms of the shape $\lambda \x.L$, such that $\x\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1}FV_i(\lambda \x.L)$, are replaced by $\boldsymbol{\lambda} \x.L$.
nodes.statement_short: Marks every abstraction whose bound variable still occurs free by turning $\lambda$ into $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$.

nodes.name: Strong normalization of $R$ transfers to $\sigma\pi\alpha$
nodes.statement: If $R$ is strongly normalizing on the sets of ground terms and ground substitutions, then $\sigma\pi\alpha$ is strongly normalizing (on the sets of terms, substitutions, and judgements of the form $\Gamma\vdash M$).
nodes.statement_short: If $R$ terminates on ground terms, so does $\sigma\pi\alpha$ on terms, substitutions and judgements.
assumptions: If $R$ is strongly normalizing on the sets of ground terms and ground substitutions
conclusions: then $\sigma\pi\alpha$ is strongly normalizing (on the sets of terms, substitutions, and judgements of the form $\Gamma\vdash M$)

nodes.name: Proof that strong normalization of $R$ transfers to $\sigma\pi\alpha$
nodes.statement:
Suppose we have some infinite $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$ M_1\arrow M_2\arrow\ldots\arrow M_n\arrow\ldots$$ I claim that we can get some infinite $R$-sequence\ $$(M_1)^*\overset{R}{	woh}(M_2)^*\overset{R}{	woh}\ldots\overset{R}{	woh}(M_n)^*\overset{R}{	woh}\ldots$$ The proof is by induction over $n$. If $n$ is equal to $1$, there is nothing to prove. Else there are three cases.\[5pt] 1) If the reduction step $ M_n\arrow M_{n+1}$ is not $Abs,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, we can apply the\ $R$-reduction of the same name $(M_n)^*\arrow( M_{n+1})^*$, but then might need several $\xi$-steps, because $ConsVar, New, ConsShift,\pi_1,\pi_2$ can decrease $FV$. If any of these reductions is applied under some black lambda, this lambda may turn pale. See Example~ef{example1.18}.\[5pt] 2) If $M_n\arrow_{\alpha_1} M_{n+1}$, we can apply $\alpha$:\ $(M_n)^*\arrow_{\alpha}(M_{n+1})^*$ (see Lemma~ef{restriction} and Example~ef{example1.13}).\[5pt] 3) If $ M_n\arrow_{Abs} M_{n+1}$ and the $Abs$-redex is $s\ci\lambda \x.M$, there are four possible subcases:\ $  egin{array}{lll} Subcase \,1. & \x
otin FV_1(\lambda \x.M),\, \x
otin FV_1(\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M);\ Subcase\, 2. & \x\in FV_1(\lambda \x.M),\, \x\in FV_1(\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M);\ Subcase\, 3. & \x
otin FV_1(\lambda \x.M),\, \x\in FV_1(\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M);\ Subcase \,4. & \x\in FV_1(\lambda \x.M),\, \x
otin FV_1(\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \xangle\ci M); \end{array}\[3pt] $ and we can apply $Abs_1, Abs_2, Abs_3$, and $Abs_4$, respectively. See Examples~ef{example1.14}, ef{example1.15}, ef{example1.16}, and ef{example1.17}. The proof is similar for substitutions. For judgements, suppose we have some infinite $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$\Gamma_1\vdash M_1i\Gamma_2\vdash M_2i\Gamma_3\vdash M_3i\ldots$$ We can obtain the $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence of terms $$\Lambda\Gamma_1.M_1	woh\Lambda\Gamma_2.M_2	woh\Lambda\Gamma_3.M_3	woh\ldots$$ where $\alpha_2$-steps are replaced by $\alpha_1$ and $Abs$.
nodes.statement_short: Map an infinite $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence to an infinite $R$-sequence through the blackening $(-)^*$.

nodes.name: A $\xi$-step is needed when $FV$ shrinks
nodes.statement: The $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$\lambda x.\la id\mi\pi_x\ci x\is x\ra\ci y\arrow_{New}\lambda x.id\ci y\arrow\ldots$$ becomes the following $R$-sequence $$\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\la id\mi\pi_x\ci x\is x\ra\ci y\arrow_{New} \boldsymbol{\lambda} x.id\ci y \arrow_{\xi}\lambda x.id\ci y\arrow\ldots$$
nodes.statement_short: After $New$ the marked abstraction must be bleached by $\xi$.

nodes.name: An $\alpha_1$-step replayed as the $R$-rule $\alpha$
nodes.statement: The $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x\arrow_{\alpha_1}\lambda y.\la\pi_y\mi y\is x\ra\ci\pi_x\ci x\arrow\ldots$$ becomes the following $R$-sequence $$\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\pi_x\ci x\arrow_{\alpha}\lambda y.\la\pi_y\mi y\is x\ra\ci\pi_x\ci x\arrow\ldots$$
nodes.statement_short: $\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\pi_x\ci x\arrow_{\alpha}\lambda y.\la\pi_y\mi y\is x\ra\ci\pi_x\ci x$.

nodes.name: Subcase 1: an $Abs$-step replayed as $Abs1$
nodes.statement: The $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$id\ci\lambda x.x\arrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\la\pi_x\ci id\mi x\is x\ra\ci x\arrow\ldots$$ becomes the following $R$-sequence $$ id\ci\lambda x.x\arrow_{Abs1}\lambda x.\la\pi_x\ci id\mi x\is x\ra\ci x\arrow\ldots$$
nodes.statement_short: Neither side is marked, so the plain rule applies.

nodes.name: Subcase 2: an $Abs$-step replayed as $Abs2$
nodes.statement: The $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$id\ci\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x\arrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\la\pi_x\ci id\mi x\is x\ra\ci\pi_x\ci x\arrow\ldots$$ becomes the following $R$-sequence $$id\ci\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\pi_x\ci x\arrow_{Abs2}\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\la\pi_x\ci id\mi x\is x\ra\ci\pi_x\ci x\arrow\ldots$$
nodes.statement_short: Both sides are marked, so black-to-black is used.

nodes.name: Subcase 3: an $Abs$-step replayed as $Abs3$
nodes.statement: The $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$\la id\mi x\is y\ra\ci\lambda x.x\arrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\la\pi_x\ci\la id\mi x\is y\ra\mi x\is x\ra\ci x\arrow\ldots$$ becomes the following $R$-sequence $$\la id\mi x\is y\ra\ci\lambda x.x\arrow_{Abs3} \boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\la\pi_x\ci\la id\mi x\is y\ra\mi x\is x\ra\ci x\arrow\ldots$$
nodes.statement_short: The substitution creates a free occurrence, so the abstraction turns black.

nodes.name: Subcase 4: an $Abs$-step replayed as $Abs4$
nodes.statement: The $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$\la id\mi\lambda y.y\is x\ra\ci\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x\arrow_{Abs}\lambda x.\la\pi_x\ci\la id\mi\lambda y.y\is x\ra\mi x\is x\ra\ci\pi_x\ci x\arrow\ldots$$ becomes the following $R$-sequence $$\la id\mi\lambda y.y\is x\ra\ci\boldsymbol{\lambda} x.\pi_x\ci x\arrow_{Abs4}\lambda x.\la\pi_x\ci\la id\mi\lambda y.y\is x\ra\mi x\is x\ra\ci\pi_x\ci x\arrow\ldots$$
nodes.statement_short: The substitution removes the free occurrence, so the abstraction turns pale.

nodes.name: The measures $|M|$ and $|s|$
nodes.statement: To each term $M$ and each substitution $s$ we put in correspondence natural numbers $|M|$ and $|s|$ respectively defined as follows:\\ $\begin{array}{l} |\lambda \x.M|=|M|+1\\ |\boldsymbol{\lambda} \x.M|=|M|+1\\ |s\ci M|=|s|+|M|\\ |s\ci q|=|s|+|q|\\ |MN|=max(|M|,|N|)\\ |\la s\mi N\is \x\ra|=max(|s|,|N|)\\ |id|=0\\ |\pi_{\x}|=0\\ |\x|=0 \end{array}$
nodes.statement_short: A natural-number measure counting nested abstractions and summing over composition and closure.

nodes.name: Signature of the rewriting system $Q$
nodes.statement: The signature of $Q$ contains:\\ $ \begin{array}{ll} M,N,L,\ldots & \text{variables};\\ s,q,r,\ldots & \text{variables};\\ x,y,z,\ldots & \text{constants};\\ id,\pi_x,\pi_y,\pi_z,\ldots &\text{constants};\\ \lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z,\ldots & \text{functional symbols of arity one};\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_i x,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i y,\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i z,\ldots & \text{functional symbols of arity one};\\ \cdot\mi\circ_i & \text{functional symbols of arity two};\\ \la -\mi -\is x\ra,\la -\mi -\is y\ra,\la -\mi -\is z\ra,\ldots & \text{functional symbols of arity two}; \end{array} $ \\[5pt] where $i\in \mathbb{N},i\geqslant 0$.\\[5pt] We will omit $\cdot$, which denotes application. The sets of ground terms and ground substitutions of $Q$ are defined inductively as follows: \begin{align*} M,N::&= \x \mid MN \mid \lambda \x. M \mid\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i \x. M\mid s\ci_i M \\ s,q::&= id \mid \pi_{\x} \mid \langle s\mi N\is \x \rangle \mid s\ci_i q \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The signature of $R$ with $\circ$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda} \x$ labelled by natural numbers.

nodes.name: $Q$ is strongly normalizing
nodes.statement: $Q$ is strongly normalizing on the sets of ground terms and ground substitutions.
conclusions: $Q$ is strongly normalizing on the sets of ground terms and ground substitutions.

nodes.name: Proof that $Q$ is strongly normalizing
nodes.statement: By choosing the well-founded precedence\\ $ \begin{array}{ll} \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{i+1} \x>\ci_i>\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i \x & \text{for all } i,\x;\\ \ci_i>\lambda \x & \text{for all } i,\x;\\ \ci_i>\cdot &\text{for all } i;\\ \ci_i>\la -\mi -\is \x\ra & \text{for all } i,\x;\\ \ci_i>\pi_{\x} & \text{for all } i,\x;\\ \ci_i> \x & \text{for all } i,\x;\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_i \x>\lambda \y & \text{for all } i,\x,\y;\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{i} \x>\la-\mi -\is \x\ra & \text{for all } i,\x;\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{i} \x>\pi_{\y} & \text{for all } i,\x,\y;\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{i} \x> \y & \text{for all } i,\x,\y;\\ \boldsymbol{\lambda}_i \x>\boldsymbol{\lambda}_j \x & \text{for } i>j; \\ \ci_i>\ci_j & \text{for } i>j; \end{array} $\\[5pt] termination is easily proved by the lexicographic path order.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit a well-founded precedence and apply the lexicographic path order.

nodes.name: $R$ is strongly normalizing
nodes.statement: $R$ is strongly normalizing on the sets of ground terms and ground substitutions.
conclusions: $R$ is strongly normalizing on the sets of ground terms and ground substitutions.

nodes.name: Proof that $R$ is strongly normalizing
nodes.statement: For any infinite $R$-sequence $$M_1\arrow M_2\arrow M_3\arrow\ldots$$ we can get some infinite $Q$-sequence simply by labelling all symbols $\circ$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda} \x$ by theirs own values. See~\cite{Zantema}, Theorem~81 for details (see also~\cite{Zantema}, Example~33). The proof is similar for substitutions.
nodes.statement_short: Label every $\circ$ and $\boldsymbol{\lambda} \x$ by its own value to turn an infinite $R$-sequence into an infinite $Q$-sequence.

nodes.name: Free variables of substitutions
nodes.statement: (Free variables of substitutions). By definition, put \\ $ \begin{array}{ll} (i) & FV(id)=\langle \emptyset,\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle\\ (ii) & FV(\pi_{\x})=\langle \emptyset,\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle\\ (iii) & FV(\la s\mi N\is \x\ra)=FV(s)\cup FV(N)\\ (iv) & FV(s\ci q)=O_s(FV(q)) \end{array} $

nodes.name: $\alpha$-equivalence for substitutions
nodes.statement: ($\alpha$-equivalence for substitutions).\\ We say that $\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta$ is $\alpha$-\emph{equal} to $\Sigma\vdash q\tri\Psi$ and write\\ $(\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta)\alp(\Sigma\vdash q\tri\Psi)$ iff\\ $(\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta)\Rightarrow (m\vdash u)$ and\\ $(\Sigma\vdash q\tri\Psi)\Rightarrow (m\vdash u)$, for some $m,u$.

nodes.name: $(x,y\vdash\pi_y\tri x)\alp (x,x\vdash \pi_x\tri x)$
nodes.statement: $ $\\ $(x,y\vdash\pi_y\tri x)\Rightarrow(2\vdash \pi)$\\ $(x,x\vdash\pi_x\tri x)\Rightarrow(2\vdash\pi)$\\ $(x,y\vdash\pi_y\tri x)\alp (x,x\vdash \pi_x\tri x)$

nodes.name: Stoughton's rule for moving a substitution under a binder
nodes.statement: According to~\cite{Stoughton}, the substitution $s$ moves under a binder this way $$(\lambda x.M)[s]\arrow\lambda y.(M[s\mi x/y])$$ where $y$ is a ``fresh" variable.
nodes.statement_short: Substitution under $\lambda x$ renames the binder to a fresh $y$ and extends $s$ with $x/y$.

nodes.name: The Abadi-Cardelli-Curien-Levy equality for abstraction
nodes.statement: They have obtained the equality $$(\lambda x.M)[s]=\lambda x.(M[(x/ x)\cdot(s\,\ci\!\uparrow)])$$
nodes.statement_short: With the shift $\uparrow$, a substitution may be pushed under a binder without renaming it.

nodes.name: Untyped terms and substitutions with unsubscripted $\pi$
nodes.statement: The sets of untyped terms and substitutions are defined inductively as follows: \begin{align*} M,N::&= x \mid MN \mid \lambda x. M \mid s\ci M \\ s,q::&= id \mid \pi \mid \langle s\mi N\is x \rangle \mid s\ci q \end{align*} where the symbol $x$ denotes an arbitrary variable.
nodes.statement_short: First-pass grammar: terms from variables, application, abstraction and closure; substitutions from $id$, $\pi$, cons and composition.

nodes.name: Judgement of the typed calculus
nodes.statement: A \emph{judgement} is an expression of the form $\Gamma\vdash M:A$ or of the form $\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta$, where $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ are contexts, $A$ is a type, $M$ is a term, and $s$ is a substitution.
differentia: of the form $\Gamma\vdash M:A$ or of the form $\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta$

nodes.name: Every derivable judgement has a unique derivation
nodes.statement: The typing rules~\ref{type} have a pleasant property: every derivable judgement has a unique derivation. This is not true for the usual typing rules because of weakening rules.
nodes.statement_short: Absence of weakening rules makes derivations unique, which is what lets the categorical semantics be defined by induction.
conclusions: every derivable judgement has a unique derivation

nodes.name: $\pi\ci M$ and $M$ have a common reduct when $y$ is absent from $\Gamma$
nodes.statement: If the variable $y$ does not occur in the context $\Gamma$, then $\pi\circ M$ reduces to $M$ in some sense (more precisely, $\pi\circ M$ and $M$ have a common reduct).
assumptions: the variable $y$ does not occur in the context $\Gamma$
conclusions: $\pi\circ M$ reduces to $M$ in some sense (more precisely, $\pi\circ M$ and $M$ have a common reduct)

nodes.name: Why rule $(ii)$ needs its side condition
nodes.statement: The restriction in the rule $(ii)$ is necessary because $\Gamma\vdash x:A$ means ``the rightmost occurrences of the variable $x$ in the context $\Gamma$ has type $A$."

nodes.name: The derived rule $(\pi)$
nodes.statement: Applying $New$ to the right part, we obtain\\ $ \begin{array}{lccc} \quad(\pi)& \qquad & \lambda x.y=\lambda x.\pi\ci y & \quad(x\not\equiv y)\\ [5pt] \end{array}$
nodes.statement_short: Combining $(\alpha)$ with $New$ yields $\lambda x.y=\lambda x.\pi\ci y$ for $x\not\equiv y$.

nodes.name: Reducts of well-formed terms and substitutions are well-formed
nodes.statement: Reducts of well-formed terms and substitutions are well-formed, hence reducts of usual $\lambda$-terms are well-formed. We will work only with well-formed terms and substitutions.
conclusions: Reducts of well-formed terms and substitutions are well-formed, hence reducts of usual $\lambda$-terms are well-formed

nodes.name: Level of a free occurrence
nodes.statement: Consider some term $M$ and some variable $\x$. To each free occurrence of $\x$ in $M$ assign its \emph{level}, which is a natural number $\geqslant 1$. The only occurrence of $x$ in the term $x$ has level $1$. We can immediately bind this occurrence and get $\lambda x.x$. The only occurrence of $x$ in the term $\pi_y\ci x$ has level $2$. We can write the term $\lambda x.\pi_y\ci x$, but this term is not well-formed (see Example~\ref{notwellformterm}). If we want to bind this occurrence and get a well-formed term, we must write $\lambda x y.\pi_y\ci x$, hence the level is $2$. The only occurrence of $x$ in the term $\pi_z\ci\pi_y\ci x$ has level $3$. The simplest way to bind this occurrence and get a well-formed term is $\lambda x y z.\pi_z\ci\pi_y\ci x$. Subscripts of the symbols $\pi_a$ are not considered as free occurrences.
nodes.statement_short: The level of a free occurrence is the number of binders needed to bind it in a well-formed way.

nodes.name: The sequence $FV(L)$ and the set of free variables of $L$
nodes.statement: In fact, we need only finite sets whose elements are variables. To each term $L$ we assign an infinite sequence of sets $$FV(L)\equiv\langle FV_1(L),FV_2(L),FV_3(L),\ldots\rangle\in Sets^\omega$$ The variables from the set $FV_i(L)$ have free occurrences of level $i$ in $L$. The set of free variables of $L$ is $\bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(L)$.
nodes.definiendum: the set of free variables of $L$

nodes.name: Warning: a bound variable can stay free
nodes.statement: Warning! May be that $\x\in\bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(\lambda \x.M)$.

nodes.name: $\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x$ is $\alpha$-equal to $\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x$
nodes.statement: In fact, the term $\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x$ is $\alpha$-equal to $\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x$.

nodes.name: $(Abs)$ rewritten with $\Uparrow_{\x}$
nodes.statement: Note that $(Abs)$ can be written as\\ $ \begin{array}{ll} (Abs) & s\ci \lambda \x.M\rightarrow\lambda \x.\!\Uparrow_{\x}\!(s) \ci M \end{array} $

nodes.name: Decomposition of $\Uparrow_{\Sigma,\x}$
nodes.statement: Note that $\Uparrow_{\Sigma,\x}\!(s)\equiv\,\Uparrow_{\x}\!\!(\Uparrow_{\Sigma}\!(s))$.

nodes.name: The terms $N_1,\ldots,N_k$ in a normal-form substitution are themselves normal
nodes.statement: Of course, the terms $N_1,\ldots,N_k$ are not arbitrary, they are $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal forms (with respect to $\arrow$).

nodes.name: The classification proof avoids $\pi_1,\pi_2,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$
nodes.statement: Note that we do not use $\pi_1,\pi_2,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ in this proof.

nodes.name: Warning: the $N_i$ of a normal-form substitution need not be pure
nodes.statement: Warning! In general, the terms $N_1,\ldots,N_k$ in the statement of Theorem~\ref{Subnf} are not pure. For example, the judgement\\ $x,x\vdash\la id\mi\pi_x\ci x\is y\ra\tri x,x,y$\\ is derivable and the substitution\\ $\la id\mi\pi_x\ci x\is y\ra$\\ is a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form.
nodes.statement_short: A counterexample: $\la id\mi\pi_x\ci x\is y\ra$ is a normal-form substitution whose component is not pure.

nodes.name: Small numerals and the recursion for $\underline{n}$
nodes.statement: We see that $\underline{1}\equiv 1$, $\underline{2}\equiv\pi\ci 1$, and $\underline{n+1}\equiv\sigma(\pi\ci\underline{n})$.

nodes.name: $m$ as the length of an invisible context
nodes.statement: Informally, $m$ is ``the length of an invisible context".

nodes.name: Warning: $\pi_1$ and $\alpha_1$ apply to different members of an $\alpha$-class
nodes.statement: Warning! We can apply $\pi_1$ to the term $\lambda x.\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x$, but not to the term $\lambda x.\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x$ (and we can apply $\alpha_1$ to the term $\lambda x.\lambda x.\pi_x\ci x$, but not to the term $\lambda x.\lambda y.\pi_y\ci x$).
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha$-equal judgements need not admit the same reduction rules.

nodes.name: Both reductions are confluent up to $\alp$ on $\Lambda\pi$
nodes.statement: We see that $\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}$ and $\overset{\sigma\pi\alpha}{\ri\ri}$ are confluent (up to $\alp$) on the set $\Lambda\pi$.

nodes.name: $\subseteq$ implies $\sqsubseteq$
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{B}$ implies $\mathcal{A} \sqsubseteq \mathcal{B}$.

nodes.name: Every function symbol of $R$ becomes a monotone function on $\mathbb{N}$
nodes.statement: Note that any functional symbol of $R$ now turns to some monotone function of $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$ or of $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Post canonical system: alphabet and predicates
nodes.statement: In this section we consider some Post canonical system building the sets of terms and substitutions. The alphabet of the system contains:\\[3pt] $ \begin{array}{ll} x\mid y\mid z\mid \lambda\mid .\mid \ci\mid id\mid \pi\mid \la\mid \mi\mid\ra\mid (\mid ) & symbols\\ \term\mid \sub\mid \var\mid \appterm\mid \absterm\mid \closterm\mid \conssub\mid \compsub \mid \varlist\mid \slist & symbols\\ a\mid b\mid M\mid N\mid s\mid q\mid G & variables \end{array}$\\[5pt] $\term M$ means that $M$ is a term. $\sub s$ means that $s$ is a substitution. $\var a$ means that $a$ is a variable. $\appterm M$ means that $M$ is a term of the form $M_1M_2\ldots M_n$, where $n\geqslant 2$. $\absterm M$ means that $M$ is a term of the form $\lambda a_1\ldots a_n.N$, where $n\geqslant 1$. $\closterm M$ means that $M$ is a term of the form $s\ci N$. $\conssub s$ means that $s$ is a substitution of the form $\la q\mi N_1\is a_1,\ldots,N_n\is a_n\ra$, where $n\geqslant 1$. $\compsub s$ means that $s$ is a substitution of the form $s_1\ci s_2\ci\ldots\ci s_n$, where $n\geqslant 2$. We will write $\pi_a$ instead of $\pi a$.
nodes.statement_short: Declares the alphabet and the ten predicates $\term$, $\sub$, $\var$, $\appterm$, $\absterm$, $\closterm$, $\conssub$, $\compsub$, $\varlist$, $\slist$.

a\qquad\quad \thickness=0.08em \shiftright 2em \endprooftree\\[5pt] The following rules build substitutions of the forms\\[1pt] $\la id\mi N_1\is a_1,\ldots,N_n\is a_n\ra$,\quad $\la\pi_a\mi N_1\is a_1,\ldots,N_n\is a_n\ra$,\\ and $\la s_1\ci s_2\ci\ldots\ci s_k\mi N_1\is a_1,\ldots,N_n\is a_n\ra$\\[5pt] \ruleone{\slist G}{\conssub \la id\mi G\ra}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\var a}{\slist G}{\conssub \la\pi_a\mi G\ra}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\compsub s}{\slist G}{\conssub \la s\mi G\ra}\\[5pt] The following rules build substitutions of the forms\\[1pt] $id\ci id$,\quad $\pi_a\ci id$,\quad $\la s\mi N_1\is a_1,\ldots,N_n\is a_n\ra\ci id$,\quad $(s_1\ci s_2\ci\ldots\ci s_n)\ci id$\\[5pt] $\compsub id\ci id$\\[5pt] \ruleone{\var a}{\compsub \pi_a\ci id}\\[5pt] \ruleone{\conssub s}{\compsub s\ci id}\\[5pt] \ruleone{\compsub s}{\compsub (s)\ci id}\\[5pt] The following rules build substitutions of the forms\\[1pt] $id\ci\pi_a$,\quad $\pi_b\ci\pi_a$,\quad $\la s\mi N_1\is a_1,\ldots,N_n\is a_n\ra\ci\pi_a$,\quad $(s_1\ci s_2\ci\ldots\ci s_n)\ci\pi_a$\\[5pt] \ruleone{\var a}{\compsub id\ci\pi_a}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\var b}{\var a}{\compsub\pi_b\ci\pi_a}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\conssub s}{\var a}{\compsub s\ci\pi_a}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\compsub s}{\var a}{\compsub (s)\ci\pi_a}\\[5pt] The following rules build substitutions of the forms\\[1pt] $id\ci\la q\mi M_1\is b_1,\ldots,M_k\is b_k\ra$,\quad $\pi_a\ci\la q\mi M_1\is b_1,\ldots,M_k\is b_k\ra$,\\ $\la s\mi N_1\is a_1,\ldots,N_n\is a_n\ra\ci\la q\mi M_1\is b_1,\ldots,M_k\is b_k\ra$,\\ and $(s_1\ci s_2\ci\ldots\ci s_n)\ci\la q\mi M_1\is b_1,\ldots,M_k\is b_k\ra$\\[5pt] \ruleone{\conssub q}{\compsub id\ci q}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\var a}{\conssub q}{\compsub \pi_a\ci q}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\conssub s}{\conssub q}{\compsub s\ci q}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\compsub s}{\conssub q}{\compsub (s)\ci q}\\[5pt] The following rules build substitutions of the forms\\[1pt] $id\ci q_1\ci q_2\ci\ldots\ci q_k$,\quad $\pi_a\ci q_1\ci q_2\ci\ldots\ci q_k$,\\ $\la s\mi N_1\is a_1,\ldots, N_n\is a_n\ra\ci q_1\ci q_2\ci\ldots\ci q_k$,\\ and $(s_1\ci s_2\ci\ldots\ci s_n)\ci q_1\ci q_2\ci\ldots\ci q_k$\\[5pt] \ruleone{\compsub q}{\compsub id\ci q}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\var a}{\compsub q}{\compsub \pi_a\ci q}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\conssub s}{\compsub q}{\compsub s\ci q}\\[5pt] \ruletwo{\compsub s}{\compsub q}{\compsub (s)\ci q}
nodes.statement_short: Productions generating every term and substitution exactly once, grouped by the shape of the head and of the argument.
nodes.section: 11 Post canonical system for terms and substitutions

nodes.name: Note (1): a stronger $Abs$ and two extra rules may be adopted
nodes.statement: (1) We can accept $Abs$ in the stronger form\\ $\begin{array}{lll} & s\ci\lambda \x.M\arrow\lambda \y.\la\pi_{\y}\ci s\mi \y\is \x\ra\ci M & (\x,\y \text{ are arbitrary}) \end{array}$\\[5pt] All results of this article remain true. We can also add the following rewrite rules\\ $\begin{array}{ll} & id\ci M\arrow M\\ & id\ci s\arrow s \end{array}$\\[5pt] All results of this article remain true.
nodes.statement_short: $Abs$ may rename the binder arbitrarily, and $id\ci M\arrow M$, $id\ci s\arrow s$ may be added, without affecting any result.

nodes.name: Note (2): an $\alpha_2$-like rule for substitutions is of little benefit
nodes.statement: (2) It is easy to add some $\alpha_2$-like reduction for substitutions, but that little benefit, because the analogue of Lemma~\ref{lemmauparrow} is false for substitutions.

nodes.name: $FV(s)$ as the image of the empty sequence
nodes.statement: We see that $FV(s)=O_s(\langle \emptyset,\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle)$

nodes.name: Case $s\equiv id$
nodes.statement: Case 1: $s$ is $id$. This implies that $\Delta$ coincides with $\Gamma$.\\
nodes.statement_short: For $s=id$ the target context coincides with $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Case $s\equiv\pi_{\x}$
nodes.statement: Case 2: $s$ has the form $\pi_{\x}$ for some $\x$. This implies that $\Gamma$ coincides with $\Delta,\x$.\\
nodes.statement_short: For $s=\pi_{\x}$ the source context must be $\Delta,\x$.

nodes.name: Case $s\equiv\la q\mi N\is \x\ra$
nodes.statement: Case 3: $s$ has the form $\langle q\mi N\is \x\rangle$ for some $q,N,\x$. By Generation lemma, we can derive $\Gamma\vdash q\tri\Sigma$ for some $\Sigma$. By the induction hypothesis, $\Sigma$ is uniquely defined for $\Gamma$ and $q$. Then $\Delta$ coincides with $\Sigma,\x$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Generation lemma and the induction hypothesis to $q$, then append $\x$.

nodes.name: Case $s\equiv q\ci r$
nodes.statement: Case 4: $s$ has the form $q\ci r$ for some $q,r$. By Generation lemma, we can derive $\Gamma\vdash q\tri\Sigma$ for some $\Sigma$. By the induction hypothesis, $\Sigma$ is uniquely defined for $\Gamma$ and $q$. By Generation lemma, we can derive $\Sigma\vdash r\tri\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is uniquely defined for $\Sigma$ and $r$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the induction hypothesis through the intermediate context $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Case $Beta$
nodes.statement: Case $Beta. \quad (\lambda \x.M)N\rightarrow \langle id\mi N\is \x\rangle\ci M $\\[5pt] $$\ruletwo{\ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma,\x\vdash M}}{\Gamma\vdash\lambda \x.M}}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash N}}{\Gamma\vdash (\lambda \x.M)N}$$\\[5pt] $$\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\Gamma\vdash id\tri\Gamma}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash N}}{\Gamma\vdash\la id\mi N\is \x\ra\tri\Gamma,\x}}{\ruledot{\Gamma,\x\vdash M}}{\Gamma\vdash\la id\mi N\is \x\ra\ci M}$$\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: Rebuild the derivation of $\la id\mi N\is \x\ra\ci M$ from those of $\lambda \x.M$ and $N$.

nodes.name: Case $Abs$
nodes.statement: Case $Abs. \quad s\ci \lambda \x.M\rightarrow\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \x\rangle\ci M $\\[5pt] $$\ruletwo{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta}}{\ruleone{\ruledot{\Delta,\x\vdash M}}{\Delta\vdash\lambda \x.M}}{\Gamma\vdash s\ci\lambda \x.M}$$\\[5pt] $$\ruleone{\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\Gamma,\x\vdash\pi_{\x}\tri\Gamma}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash s\tri\Delta}}{\Gamma,\x\vdash\pi_{\x}\ci s\tri\Delta}}{\Gamma,\x\vdash \x}{\Gamma,\x\vdash\la\pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \x\ra\tri\Delta,\x}}{\ruledot{\Delta,\x\vdash M}}{\Gamma,\x\vdash\la\pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \x\ra\ci M}}{\Gamma\vdash\lambda \x.\la\pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \x\ra\ci M}$$\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: Rebuild the derivation after pushing $s$ under the binder as $\la\pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \x\ra$.

nodes.name: Case $\alpha_1$
nodes.statement: Case $\alpha_1$. $ \lambda \x.M\rightarrow\lambda \y.\langle\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\rangle\ci M $ $\quad (*)$ \\[5pt] $$\ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma,\x\vdash M}}{\Gamma\vdash\lambda \x.M}$$\\[5pt] $$\ruleone{\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\Gamma,\y\vdash\pi_{\y}\tri\Gamma}{\Gamma,\y\vdash \y}{\Gamma,\y\vdash\la\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\ra\tri\Gamma,\x}}{\ruledot{\Gamma,\x\vdash M}}{\Gamma,\y\vdash\la\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\ra\ci M}}{\Gamma\vdash\lambda \y.\la\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\ra\ci M}$$\\[5pt] And so on. Note that we do not use $(*)$ in the proof of the case $\alpha_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Rebuild the derivation for the renamed abstraction; the side condition $(*)$ is not needed.

nodes.name: Case $q\equiv id$
nodes.statement: Case 1: $q$ is $id$.\\ $s\ci id\arrow s$\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: $IdR$ collapses $s\ci id$ to $s$.

nodes.name: Case $s\equiv id$, $q$ a $\pi$-chain
nodes.statement: Case 2: $s$ is $id$ and $q$ has the form $\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$.\\ $id\ci \pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}\twoh \pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: $IdShift$ removes the leading $id$.

nodes.name: Case both are $\pi$-chains
nodes.statement: Case 3: $s$ has the form $\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n}$ and $q$ has the form $\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$.\\ $(\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n})\ci\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}\twoh \pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n\z_1\ldots\z_m}$\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: Two $\pi$-chains concatenate into one.

nodes.name: Case $s$ a cons, $q$ a $\pi$-chain
nodes.statement: Case 4: $s$ has the form $\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra$ and $q$ has the form $\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$, where $r$ is $id$ or $\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n}$. Hence, $s\circ q$ has the form\\ $\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra\ci\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$. By Generation lemma, $\y_k= \z_1$,\\ $\y_{k-1}= \z_2$, and so on (see Example~\ref{bedsubst}). \\[5pt] If $k=m$,\,then\\[5pt] $\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra\ci\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$\quad is the same as\\ $\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra\ci\pi_{\y_k\ldots\y_1}\twoh r$\\[5pt] If $k>m$,\,then \\[5pt] $\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra\ci\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$\quad is the same as\\ $\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra\ci\pi_{\y_k\ldots\y_{k-m+1}}\twoh \la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_{k-m}\is \y_{k-m}\ra $\\[5pt] If $k<m$,\,then\\[5pt] $\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra\ci\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$\quad is the same as\\ $\la r\mi N_1\is \z_k\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \z_1\ra\ci\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$\\ If $r$ is $id$, this term reduces to $\pi_{\z_{k+1}\ldots\z_m}$. If $r$ is $\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n}$, this term reduces to $\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n\z_{k+1}\ldots\z_m}$.\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: Generation forces the consed variables to match the chain; compare $k$ with $m$.

nodes.name: Case $q$ a cons
nodes.statement: Case 5: $q$ has the form $\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra$, where $r$ is $id$ or $\pi_{\z_1\ldots\z_m}$.\\ $s\ci\la r\mi N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi N_k\is \y_k\ra\twoh\la s\ci r\mi s\ci N_1\is \y_1\mi\ldots\mi s\ci N_k\is \y_k\ra$\\ Then we use the previous cases to reduce $s\ci r$.
nodes.statement_short: $Map$ distributes $s$ over the cons, reducing to the earlier cases.

nodes.name: Reduce to a variable argument
nodes.statement: Suppose $M$ contain a sub-term of the shape $s\ci N$; then $N$ must be a variable (we denote it by $\y$), else we can apply $Abs, App$ or $Clos$.
nodes.statement_short: If the argument of a closure is not a variable, $Abs$, $App$ or $Clos$ applies.

nodes.name: Force $s$ to be a $\pi$-chain
nodes.statement: The substitution $s$ is a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form and must have the form $\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n}$ (see theorem~\ref{Subnf}), else we can apply $IdVar, ConsVar$ or $New$.
nodes.statement_short: By the normal-form theorem for substitutions, $s$ must be $\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n}$.

nodes.name: Force the last subscript to match
nodes.statement: Further, $\x_n$ in $(\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_n})\ci \y$ must coincide with $\y$, else we can apply $\pi_1$ or $\pi_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise $\pi_1$ or $\pi_2$ applies.

nodes.name: Reduce to blocks and defer
nodes.statement: We see that $M$ must be constructed from variables and blocks of the form $(\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_m\y})\ci \y\quad (m\geqslant 0)$ by using application and abstraction. To conclude the proof, it is sufficient to prove the following lemma.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is built from variables and blocks $(\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_m\y})\ci \y$; the next lemma finishes.

nodes.name: Case $M$ a variable
nodes.statement: Case 1: $M$ is a variable. The proof is trivial.\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: Trivial: a variable is pure.

nodes.name: Case $M$ a block
nodes.statement: Case 2: $ M$ has the form $(\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_m\y})\ci \y$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma\vdash M$ has the form\\ $\Delta\mi\y\mi\x_m\mi\ldots\mi \x_1\vdash (\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_m\y})\ci \y$ \\ and we can apply $\alpha_2$ , because\\ $FV(\y\mi\x_m\mi\ldots\mi \x_1\vdash (\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_m\y})\ci \y)=\la\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\ra$\\[10pt]
nodes.statement_short: Generation pins the context shape, and the free-variable computation licenses $\alpha_2$.

nodes.name: Case $M\equiv\lambda \x.N$
nodes.statement: Case 3: $M$ has the form $\lambda \x.N$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma,\x\vdash N$ is derivable. Suppose $N$ contains a block of the form $(\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_m\y})\ci \y$. By induction hypothesis, we can apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma,\x\vdash N$. But any application of $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma,\x\vdash N$ corresponds to some application of $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ (and, in some cases, $Abs$) to $\Gamma\vdash\lambda \x.N$. For example,\\ $\Gamma,\x\vdash N\ri_{\alpha_2}\Gamma,\y \vdash\la\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\ra\ci N$\\ corresponds to\\ $\Gamma\vdash\lambda \x.N\ri_{\alpha_1}\Gamma\vdash\lambda \y.\la\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\ra\ci N$\\[10pt]
nodes.statement_short: An $\alpha_1$/$\alpha_2$ step inside $N$ lifts to one on $\lambda \x.N$.

nodes.name: Case $M\equiv NL$
nodes.statement: Case 4: $M$ has the form $NL$. By Generation lemma, $\Gamma\vdash N$ and $\Gamma\vdash L$ are derivable. Suppose one of these terms contains a block of the form $(\pi_{\x_1\ldots\x_m\y})\ci \y$. For clarity, let it be $N$. By induction hypothesis, we can apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash N$. I claim that we can apply $\alpha_1$ or $\alpha_2$ to $\Gamma\vdash NL$. For the case $\alpha_1$ is nothing to prove, because any $\alpha_1$-redex in $N$ occurs in $NL$ too. For the case $\alpha_2$, suppose that $\Gamma\vdash NL$ has the form $\Sigma,\x,\Delta\vdash NL$. Recall that $FV(NL)=FV(N)\cup FV(L)$, hence $FV(N)\subseteq FV(NL)$. By Lemma~\ref{monotone},\\ $FV(\x,\Delta\vdash N))\subseteq FV(\x,\Delta\vdash NL)$.\\ Hence if $\x\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(\x,\Delta\vdash N)$, then $\x\in \bigcup_{i\geqslant 1} FV_i(\x,\Delta\vdash NL)$. If we can apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,\x,\Delta\vdash N$, then we can apply $\alpha_2$ to $\Sigma,\x,\Delta\vdash NL$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $FV$ transfers the applicability of $\alpha_2$ from $N$ to $NL$.

nodes.name: Set up derivability and purity
nodes.statement: $\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable by Lemma~\ref{poleznaya}. $\Sigma\vdash L$ is derivable by Subject reduction. Therefore $L$ is pure and $V$ is a $\sigma$-normal form (Theorem~\ref{pure}, Lemma~\ref{purelemma}). Why $U\overset{\sigma}{\twoh}V$? It is sufficient to prove that $\sigma(U)\equiv\sigma(V)$ ($U$ reduces to its $\sigma$-normal form because $\sigma$ is strongly normalizing and confluent).
nodes.statement_short: Both endpoints are derivable, so $L$ is pure and $V$ is a $\sigma$-normal form.

nodes.name: Induct on the reduction length
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction over the length of the reduction sequence $ \Gamma\vdash M\overset{\sigma\pi\alpha}{\ri\ri}\Sigma\vdash L$. If this length is equal to $0$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, suppose this sequence has the form \\ $\Gamma\vdash M\ri\ldots\ri\Delta\vdash N\ri\Sigma\vdash L$,\\ where $(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}W$ and $\sigma(U)\equiv\sigma(W)$.\\ Any possible $\sigma\pi\alpha$-reduction step $\Delta\vdash N\ri\Sigma\vdash L$, except $New,\pi_1,\pi_2,\alpha_1$, and $\alpha_2$ corresponds to the same name $\sigma$-reduction step of the nameless terms $W\arrow V$, hence $\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in these cases. For $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ use Lemma~\ref{lemmauparrow}.\\
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a single step and note that ordinary steps map to $\sigma$-steps.

nodes.name: Case $\pi_1$
nodes.statement: (\textbf{Case} $\boldsymbol{\pi_1}.) \quad \pi_{\x}\ci \y\arrow \y \qquad(\x\neq \y)$ $$\ruletwo{\Gamma,\x\vdash \pi_{\x}\tri\Gamma}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash \y}}{\Gamma,\x\vdash\pi_{\x}\ci \y}\qquad \ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash \y}}{\Gamma,\x\vdash \y}$$ Suppose \\ $(\Gamma\vdash \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\ then\\ $(\Gamma,\x\vdash\pi_{\x}\ci \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\pi\ci\underline{n}$ and\\ $(\Gamma,\x\vdash \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n+1}$.\\ We see that $\sigma(\pi\ci\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(\underline{n+1})$. \\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma(\pi\ci\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(\underline{n+1})$.

nodes.name: Case $\pi_2$
nodes.statement: (\textbf{Case} $\boldsymbol{\pi_2}.) \quad (s\ci\pi_{\x})\ci \y\arrow s\ci \y \qquad(\x\neq \y)$ $$\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash s\tri\Gamma,\x}}{\Gamma,\x\vdash\pi_{\x}\tri\Gamma}{\Delta\vdash s\ci\pi_{\x}\tri\Gamma}}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash \y}}{\Delta\vdash (s\ci\pi_{\x})\ci \y}\qquad \ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash s\tri\Gamma,\x}}{\ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash \y}}{\Gamma,\x\vdash \y}}{\Delta\vdash s\ci \y}$$ Suppose \\ $(\Delta\vdash s\tri\Gamma,\x)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} u$;\\ $(\Gamma\vdash \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\ then\\ $(\Delta\vdash (s\ci\pi_{\x})\ci \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} (u\ci\pi)\ci\underline{n}$;\\ $(\Gamma,\x\vdash \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} \underline{n+1}$;\\ $(\Delta\vdash s\ci \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} u\ci\underline{n+1}$.\\ We see that\\ $\sigma((u\ci\pi)\ci\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(u\ci\underline{n+1})$\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma((u\ci\pi)\ci\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(u\ci\underline{n+1})$.

nodes.name: Case $New$
nodes.statement: (\textbf{Case} ${\mathbf{New}}.) \quad \la s\mi N\is \x\ra\ci \y\arrow s\ci \y \qquad(\x\neq \y)$ $$\ruletwo{\ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash s\tri\Gamma}}{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash N}}{\Delta\vdash\la s\mi N\is \x\ra\tri\Gamma,\x}}{\ruleone{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash \y}}{\Gamma,\x\vdash \y}}{\Delta\vdash\la s\mi N\is \x\ra\ci \y}\qquad \ruletwo{\ruledot{\Delta\vdash s\tri\Gamma}}{\ruledot{\Gamma\vdash \y}}{\Delta\vdash s\ci \y}$$ Suppose \\ $(\Delta\vdash s\tri\Gamma)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} u$;\\ $(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} V$;\\ $(\Gamma\vdash \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n}$;\\ then\\ $(\Gamma,\x\vdash \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\underline{n+1}$;\\ $(\Delta\vdash\la s\mi N\is \x\ra\ci \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\la u\mi V\ra\ci\underline{n+1}$;\\ $(\Delta\vdash s\ci \y)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} u\ci\underline{n}$.\\ We see that\\ $\sigma(\la u\mi V\ra\ci\underline{n+1})\equiv\sigma(\la u\mi V\ra\ci\pi\ci\underline{n})\equiv\sigma(u\ci\underline{n})$.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma(\la u\mi V\ra\ci\underline{n+1})\equiv\sigma(u\ci\underline{n})$.

nodes.name: Induct on the reduction length
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction over the length of the reduction sequence $\Gamma\vdash M\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma\vdash L$. If this length is equal to $0$, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, suppose this sequence has the form \\ $\Gamma\vdash M\ri\ldots\ri\Delta\vdash N\ri\Sigma\vdash L$,\\ where $(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow} W$ and $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh}\sigma(W)$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Split off the last step of the sequence.

nodes.name: Case: a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-step
nodes.statement: If the reduction step $\Delta\vdash N\ri\Sigma\vdash L$ belongs to $\sigma\pi\alpha$, everything is all right, because $\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case. Indeed, $\Gamma\vdash M$ is derivable by Lemma~\ref{poleznaya}. $\Delta\vdash N$ and $\Sigma\vdash L$ are derivable by Subject reduction. Take any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Sigma\vdash L$ (this normal form exists by Theorem ~\ref{SN} and are derivable too) and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to get $ W\overset{\sigma}{\twoh}\sigma(V)$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Normalize and apply the projection theorem to get $\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$.

nodes.name: Case: a $Beta$-step
nodes.statement: If $\Delta\vdash N\ri_{Beta}\Sigma\vdash L$, then $W\arrow_{Beta}V$, because any $Beta$-redex in $N$ corresponds to some $Beta$-redex in $W$, hence $\sigma(W)\arrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}.
nodes.statement_short: The redex lifts to the name-free side, so the lifting lemma applies.

nodes.name: Base case: empty reduction
nodes.statement: Case 1: If this length is equal to $0$, take any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Gamma\vdash M$ as $\Sigma\vdash L$ and use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem}. \\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: Take any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Gamma\vdash M$.

nodes.name: Inductive step: one more $\lambda\sigma$-step
nodes.statement: Case 2: Suppose this sequence has the form $U\arrow \ldots\arrow W\arrow V$ and the sequence $U\arrow \ldots\arrow W$ satisfies the statement of the theorem, i.e.:\\ $\Gamma\vdash M \overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Delta\vdash N$ for some $\Delta\vdash N$, where $\Delta\vdash N$ is a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form and $(\Delta\vdash N)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(W)$.\\[3pt] If the reduction step $W\arrow V$ belongs to $\sigma$, everything is all right, because $\sigma(W)\equiv\sigma(V)$ in this case and we can use $\Delta\vdash N$ as $\Sigma\vdash L$. \\[3pt] If $W\arrow_{Beta}V$, then $\sigma(W)\arrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemmapodjom}. If $\sigma(W)$ coincides with $\sigma(V)$, everything is all right. Otherwise, suppose $\sigma(W)\arrow^*_{\beta}\sigma(V)$ has the form $\sigma(W)\arrow_{Beta}W'\overset{\sigma}{\twoh}\sigma(V)$. Any $Beta$-redex in $\sigma(W)$ corresponds to some $Beta$-redex in $N$. Contracting this redex in $N$, we obtain\\ $\Delta\vdash N\ri_{Beta}\Delta\vdash N'$ and $(\Delta\vdash N')\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}W'$, for some $N'$. Take any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta\vdash N'$ as $\Sigma\vdash L$, then use Theorem~\ref{maintheorem} to obtain\\ $(\Sigma\vdash L)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma$-steps change nothing; a $Beta$-step is contracted in the corresponding redex of $N$.

nodes.name: Pass from $\alp$ to $\backsimeq$
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\backsimeq(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)$.\\ Suppose $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$ and $(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$.\\
nodes.statement_short: The two judgements have a common translation $U$.

nodes.name: Normalize both reducts
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma_1\vdash L_1$ be any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta_1\vdash N_1$ and let $\Sigma_2\vdash L_2$ be any $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form of $\Delta_2\vdash N_2$. By Theorem~\ref{maintheorem}, we have\\ $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(U)$ and $(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(U)$, hence\\ $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\backsimeq(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Both normal forms translate to $\sigma(U)$, hence are $\backsimeq$-related.

nodes.name: Return to $\alp$
nodes.statement: Note that $L_1$ and $L_2$ are pure (Theorem~\ref{pure}). Note that $|\Sigma_1|=|\Sigma_2|=|\Gamma_1|=|\Gamma_2|$ (because all reductions preserve lengths of contexts). By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have\\ $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\alp(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Purity and equal context lengths upgrade $\backsimeq$ back to $\alpha$-equality.

nodes.name: Pass from $\alp$ to $\backsimeq$
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\backsimeq(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)$.\\ Suppose $(\Gamma_1\vdash M_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$; $(\Gamma_2\vdash M_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}U$;\\ $(\Delta_1\vdash N_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}V_1$; and $(\Delta_2\vdash N_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}V_2$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Both judgements translate to the same $U$.

nodes.name: Project into $\lambda\sigma$ and join there
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{theorem33}, we have $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} \sigma(V_1)$ and $\sigma(U)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} \sigma(V_2)$.\\ We know that $\lambda\sigma$ is confluent, hence $\sigma(V_1)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} V$ and $\sigma(V_2)\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} V$ for some $V$. Therefore $V_1\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} V$ and $V_2\overset{\lambda\sigma}{\twoh} V$.
nodes.statement_short: Confluence of $\lambda\sigma$ supplies a common reduct $V$.

nodes.name: Lift the joining reductions back
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{theorem44}, we have $\Sigma_1\vdash L_1$ and $\Sigma_2\vdash L_2$ such that\\ $\begin{array}{l} \Delta_1\vdash N_1\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma_1\vdash L_1;\\ \Delta_2\vdash N_2\overset{\lambda\pi}{\ri\ri}\Sigma_2\vdash L_2;\\ \Sigma_1\vdash L_1 \text{ is a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form};\\ \Sigma_2\vdash L_2 \text{ is a $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form};\\ (\Sigma_1\vdash V_1)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V);\\ (\Sigma_2\vdash V_2)\boldsymbol{\Rightarrow}\sigma(V). \end{array}$\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: The lifting theorem produces $\Sigma_i\vdash L_i$ in $\sigma\pi\alpha$-normal form.

nodes.name: Return to $\alp$
nodes.statement: Hence $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\backsimeq(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$. Note that $L_1$ and $L_2$ are pure (Theorem~\ref{pure}). Note that $|\Sigma_1|=|\Sigma_2|=|\Gamma_1|=|\Gamma_2|$ (because all reductions preserve lengths of contexts). By Lemma~\ref{alpequiv}, we have\\ $(\Sigma_1\vdash L_1)\alp(\Sigma_2\vdash L_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Purity and equal context lengths upgrade $\backsimeq$ back to $\alpha$-equality.

nodes.name: Case $Abs$
nodes.statement: \mathbf{(Abs)} & s\ci \lambda \x.M\rightarrow\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \x\rangle\ci M & \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{ll} FV(\lambda \x.\langle \pi_{\x}\ci s\mi \x\is \x\rangle\ci M) & \\ =FV(\lambda \x.((\pi_{\x}\ci s)\ci\lambda \x.M)\x) & (Lemma~\ref{corollary3})\\ =FV(\lambda \x.(\pi_{\x}\ci s\ci\lambda \x.M)\x) & (Lemma~\ref{corollary23})\\ =O_{\lambda \x}(O_{\pi}(FV (s\ci\lambda \x.M))\bigcup FV(\x)) & \\ =O_{\lambda \x}(\la\{\x\},FV_1(s\ci\lambda \x.M),FV_2(s\ci\lambda \x.M),\ldots\ra) & \\ =FV(s\ci\lambda \x.M) \end{array}$\\ $\begin{array}{lll}
nodes.statement_short: Both sides compute to $FV(s\ci\lambda \x.M)$.

nodes.name: Case $App$
nodes.statement: \mathbf{(App)} & s\ci MN \rightarrow(s\ci M)(s\ci N) & \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{l} FV(s\ci MN) \\ =O_s(FV(MN))\\ =O_s(FV(M)\cup FV(N))\\ \supseteq O_s(FV(M))\cup O_s(FV(N))\\ =FV(s\ci M)\cup FV(s\ci N)\\ =FV((s\ci M)(s\ci N)) \end{array}$\\ $ \begin{array}{lll}
nodes.statement_short: $O_s$ of a union contains the union of the images.

nodes.name: Case $ConsVar$
nodes.statement: \mathbf{(ConsVar)} & \langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle\ci \x\rightarrow N & \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{l} FV(\langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle\ci \x)\\ =O_{\langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle}(FV(\x))\\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(FV(\x)))\cup FV(N)\\ \supseteq FV(N) \end{array}$\\ $ \begin{array}{lll}
nodes.statement_short: The cons clause of $FV$ already contains $FV(N)$.

nodes.name: Case $New$
nodes.statement: \mathbf{(New)} & \langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle\ci \y\rightarrow s\ci \y & (\x\neq \y) \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{l} FV(\langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle\ci \y)\\ =O_{\langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle}(FV(\y))\\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(FV(\y)))\cup FV(N)\\ \supseteq O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(FV(\y)))\\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(\langle\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle)\\ =O_s(\langle\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle)\\ =O_s(FV(\y))\\ =FV(s\ci \y) \end{array}$\\ $\begin{array}{lll}
nodes.statement_short: Dropping the cons component leaves exactly $FV(s\ci \y)$.

nodes.name: Case $ConsShift$
nodes.statement: \mathbf{(ConsShift)} & \langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle\ci \pi_{\x}\rightarrow s & \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{l} O_{\langle s\mi N\is \x\rangle\ci \pi_{\x}}(\mathcal{A})\\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(O_{\pi}(\mathcal{A})))\cup FV(N)\\ \supseteq O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(O_{\pi}(\mathcal{A})))\\ =O_s(O_{\lambda \x}(\langle\emptyset,\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2,\ldots\rangle)\\ =O_s(\langle\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2,\ldots\rangle)\\ =O_s(\mathcal{A}) \end{array}$\\ $ \begin{array}{lll}
nodes.statement_short: $O_{\lambda \x}$ undoes $O_{\pi}$, returning $O_s(\mathcal{A})$.

nodes.name: Case $Map$
nodes.statement: \mathbf{(Map)} & s\ci \langle q\mi N\is \x\rangle\rightarrow\langle s\ci q \mi s\ci N\is \x\rangle & \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{l} O_{s\,\ci \langle q\mi N\is \x\rangle}(\mathcal{A})\\ =O_s(O_{\langle q\mi N\is \x\rangle}(\mathcal{A}))\\ =O_s(O_q(O_{\lambda \x}(\mathcal{A}))\cup FV(N))\\ \supseteq O_s(O_q(O_{\lambda \x}(\mathcal{A})))\cup O_s(FV(N))\\ =O_{s\ci q}(O_{\lambda \x}(\mathcal{A}))\cup FV(s\ci N)\\ =O_{\langle s\ci q \mi s\ci N\is \x\rangle}(\mathcal{A}) \end{array}$\\ $ \begin{array}{lll}
nodes.statement_short: Distributing $O_s$ over the union gives the right-hand side.

nodes.name: Case $\pi_1$
nodes.statement: \boldsymbol{(\pi_1)} & \pi_{\x}\ci \y\rightarrow \y & (\x\neq \y) \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{l} FV(\pi_{\x}\ci \y)\\ =\langle\emptyset,\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle\\ \sqsupseteq \langle\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle\\ =FV(\y) \end{array}$ \\ $ \begin{array}{lll}
nodes.statement_short: $\la\emptyset,\{\y\},\ldots\ra\sqsupseteq\la\{\y\},\emptyset,\ldots\ra$.

nodes.name: Case $\pi_2$
nodes.statement: \boldsymbol{(\pi_2)} & (s\ci\pi_{\x})\ci \y\rightarrow s\ci \y & (\x\neq \y) \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{l} FV((s\ci\pi_{\x})\ci \y)\\ =O_s(O_{\pi}(FV(\y)))\\ = O_s(\langle\emptyset,\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle)\\ \sqsupseteq O_s(\langle\{\y\},\emptyset,\emptyset,\ldots\rangle)\\ =FV(s\ci \y) \end{array}$\\ $\begin{array}{lll}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the $\pi_1$ computation under $O_s$.

nodes.name: Case $\alpha_1$
nodes.statement: \boldsymbol{(\alpha_1)} & \lambda \x.M\rightarrow\lambda \y.\langle\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\rangle\ci M & (*) \end{array} $\\ $\begin{array}{ll} FV(\lambda \y.\langle\pi_{\y}\mi \y\is \x\rangle\ci M )\\ =FV(\lambda \y.(\pi_{\y}\ci\lambda \x.M)\y) & (Lemma~\ref{corollary3})\\ =O_{\lambda \y}(O_{\pi}(FV(\lambda \x.M))\bigcup FV(\y)) & \\ =O_{\lambda \y}(\la\{\y\},FV_1(\lambda \x.M),FV_2(\lambda \x.M),\ldots\ra) & \\ =FV(\lambda \x.M) \end{array} $\\[3pt]
nodes.statement_short: Renaming leaves $FV$ unchanged.

nodes.name: Remaining monotonicity obligations
nodes.statement: In addition, it is necessary to prove that all operations from Definition~\ref{pervoe} are in some sense monotone, but this is not difficult.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of the syntactic operations is noted as not difficult.

nodes.name: Case: ordinary rules
nodes.statement: 1) If the reduction step $ M_n\arrow M_{n+1}$ is not $Abs,\alpha_1,\alpha_2$, we can apply the\\ $R$-reduction of the same name $(M_n)^*\arrow( M_{n+1})^*$, but then might need several $\xi$-steps, because $ConsVar, New, ConsShift,\pi_1,\pi_2$ can decrease $FV$. If any of these reductions is applied under some black lambda, this lambda may turn pale. See Example~\ref{example1.18}.\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: Replay the rule of the same name, inserting $\xi$-steps when $FV$ shrinks.

nodes.name: Case: $\alpha_1$-steps
nodes.statement: 2) If $M_n\arrow_{\alpha_1} M_{n+1}$, we can apply $\alpha$:\\ $(M_n)^*\arrow_{\alpha}(M_{n+1})^*$ (see Lemma~\ref{restriction} and Example~\ref{example1.13}).\\[5pt]
nodes.statement_short: Replay them by the $R$-rule $\alpha$.

nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Substitutions and judgements
nodes.statement: The proof is similar for substitutions. For judgements, suppose we have some infinite $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence $$\Gamma_1\vdash M_1\ri\Gamma_2\vdash M_2\ri\Gamma_3\vdash M_3\ri\ldots$$ We can obtain the $\sigma\pi\alpha$-sequence of terms $$\Lambda\Gamma_1.M_1\twoh\Lambda\Gamma_2.M_2\twoh\Lambda\Gamma_3.M_3\twoh\ldots$$ where $\alpha_2$-steps are replaced by $\alpha_1$ and $Abs$.
nodes.statement_short: Judgement sequences become term sequences by abstracting the context, turning $\alpha_2$ into $\alpha_1$ plus $Abs$.
